# Creating Kubernetes compute 
A `k8s` compute is not a machine. It is a pool row holding the cluster, the namespace, the pod image and the pod's resource limits, and every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. The pod runs `arkd` as its main container and dials out to the control plane, so nothing reaches into your cluster: no inbound route, no `kubectl port-forward`, no kubeconfig read at dispatch time. When the session ends the pod is deleted.
Because the pod is created per dispatch, a k8s pool is always cold. Setting a warm floor is rejected outright with `cannot be warm (min must be 0)`. There is nothing to keep warm.

Tool caching takes one decision. By default each workspace gets a ReadWriteOnce PVC that stays warm between sessions but pins concurrent sessions for that workspace to one node. # Onboarding 
Foundry runs coding agents on your team's repositories. You describe a piece of work, Foundry runs it through a defined process on a machine your team owns, and you get a pull request back. Many of those runs happen at once, on real hardware, rather than one at a time on your laptop.
This section gets you from nothing to your first run. You will need an account, your editor connected, and a few credentials so the work is done as you and not as a shared account.
It takes about an hour of your own time. The one thing you cannot do yourself is compute, which your DevOps sets up once for the whole team, so start that conversation early.

## Roles, and how a team comes online 
Onboarding a team comes down to one person. The platform team creates the accounts and gives one person a tenant-admin grant. From there that admin unlocks the rest for the team: they onboard everyone else, register the team's compute, and set the team's secrets, without the platform team in the loop for each step.
Ark has four roles:
  - **Member** is the everyday role. A member creates flows, agents, and workspaces, runs sessions, uses shared secrets, and edits or deletes what they created. Most people are members.
  - **Team-admin** runs one team. It does everything a member can, and manages its own team's shared resources and secrets. Its authority covers that team and its sub-teams, and nothing outside them.
  - **Tenant-admin** runs the whole tenant: onboard anyone, manage every team, register compute, an

## How scope resolution works 
Secrets resolve **narrowest first** : user, then team, then tenant, and the first hit for each name wins. A team that sets nothing inherits the tenant default.
Two consequences worth knowing before you debug a missing secret:
  - Setting a value at **user** scope overrides team and tenant for your sessions only. That makes it the fastest way to unblock yourself while a shared value is being sorted out.
  - A team-scoped secret is matched by the team's canonical `tm-` id. A value stored against the team's name or slug will be visible in the UI and still not resolve at dispatch.

Account creation (Cognito login + tenant membership) is done by the platform team - send the email and team name (or a .csv for a whole team) to a tenant admin, listed on the **Settings** page under **Your admins**. Once the user exists, you control _what they can do_ with grants:

# Creating EC2 compute 
An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. The same kind can also adopt a box you already run, in which case Foundry installs `arkd` and nothing else, as below. That is the difference from [registering a machine you already own](/onboarding/registering-compute), where the box dials in and Foundry never touches its lifecycle.
You create it in one of two shapes. A **dedicated box** is a single named instance your team's sessions land on, which is what most teams start with. A **pool** is a blueprint that cuts a fresh instance per session up to a ceiling you set, which is what you want once several people dispatch at once. ## Capacity and admission 
Admission control decides how much work a box will accept before it queues the rest, and it is on by default. When a compute declares no `capacity`, Foundry derives a conservative one from the instance size at 85% headroom, reserving the rest for the OS, `arkd`, and the agent runtime. An `m` box (8 vCPU, 32 GB) therefore admits against roughly 27Gi and 680% CPU.
An adopted box carries no size, because Foundry did not choose its instance type and will not invent one, so declaring capacity is not optional there: until you do, a workspace that declares a `resource_budget` is refused on it with a message naming exactly this. A workspace declaring no budget is not gated at all, so an uncapped adopted box will accept work regardless.

An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. # Creating EC2 compute 
An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. The same kind can also adopt a box you already run, in which case Foundry installs `arkd` and nothing else, as below. You create it in one of two shapes. A **dedicated box** is a single named instance your team's sessions land on, which is what most teams start with. A **pool** is a blueprint that cuts a fresh instance per session up to a ceiling you set, which is what you want once several people dispatch at once. **Goal:** Stop the outages before we add anything new.

- Stop 503s: credential-refresh grant for the weekly DB password rotation, plus event-consumer backpressure.

records.answer: To register your own worker to always run under Cursor, you need to write a YAML file with the worker's definition. The YAML file should include the `name` and `runtime` fields, with the `runtime` field set to `cursor`. You can then register the worker using the command `ark agent create <agent-name> --from <yaml-file> --no-editor --global`. For example: `ark agent create myteam-reviewer --from myteam-reviewer.yaml --no-editor --global`. A minimal agent YAML would include `name` and `runtime` fields, like this: `name: myteam-reviewer` and `runtime: cursor`. You can list all registered agents with `ark agent list` to confirm that your agent was registered successfully.

records.answer: You can stand up the Kubernetes pool your team's flow needs. Creating a pool is authorized at the tenant rung, so this is a tenant-admin action. A tenant can also be locked to specific clusters, in which case creating a pool elsewhere fails with `Tenant "<id>" is not permitted to target k8s cluster "<key>"`. To create a pool, you need a cluster the control plane can reach and authenticate to, a namespace for the agent pods, and an image for them. You can use the `compute` MCP tool or the `ark compute update` command to set the pool's configuration, including its capacity and resources.

## Sizing 
Four numbers decide pod size and throughput, and none of them substitutes for another:
Field| What it sets  
---|---  
`config.resources`| The `arkd` container's request and limit, in Kubernetes units (`"2"` is two cores, `"500m"` half of one). Applies when the session declares no budget of its own  
workspace `resource_budget`| What actually sizes the pod on a real dispatch, so a workspace can outgrow the pool default  
`config.sidecarResources`| Charged once per declared service, plus one for DinD, in the same pod  
`config.capacity`| The admission ledger's ceiling for the whole pool row  
The pod total is `arkd` plus every sidecar, and that total has to fit on one node after daemonsets and kube-reserved take their share, which is meaningfully less than the instance spec suggests. A workspace that asks for slightly more than a node can give never schedules at all

**Goal:** Stop the outages before we add anything new.

## Capacity and admission 
Admission control decides how much work a box will accept before it queues the rest, and it is on by default. When a compute declares no `capacity`, Foundry derives a conservative one from the instance size at 85% headroom, reserving the rest for the OS, `arkd`, and the agent runtime. An `m` box (8 vCPU, 32 GB) therefore admits against roughly 27Gi and 680% CPU.
An adopted box carries no size, because Foundry did not choose its instance type and will not invent one, so declaring capacity is not optional there: until you do, a workspace that declares a `resource_budget` is refused on it with a message naming exactly this. A workspace declaring no budget is not gated at all, so an uncapped adopted box will accept work regardless.

Foundry runs coding agents on your team's repositories. You describe a piece of work, Foundry runs it through a defined process on a machine your team owns, and you get a pull request back. Many of those runs happen at once, on real hardware, rather than one at a time on your laptop.
This section gets you from nothing to your first run. You will need an account, your editor connected, and a few credentials so the work is done as you and not as a shared account.

# Creating Kubernetes compute 
A `k8s` compute is not a machine. It is a pool row holding the cluster, the namespace, the pod image and the pod's resource limits, and every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. The pod runs `arkd` as its main container and dials out to the control plane, so nothing reaches into your cluster: no inbound route, no `kubectl port-forward`, no kubeconfig read at dispatch time. When the session ends the pod is deleted.
Because the pod is created per dispatch, a k8s pool is always cold. Setting a warm floor is rejected outright with `cannot be warm (min must be 0)`. There is nothing to keep warm.

# Set up Cursor 
Cursor shows up in Foundry in two unrelated ways, and this page covers both.
The first is Cursor as your editor: it connects to the control plane's MCP server and gets the `ark` toolbox, so you can dispatch sessions, inspect flows and steer runs without leaving Cursor. The second is Cursor as a **runtime** , one of the harnesses Foundry dispatches agents onto, alongside the `claude-agent` and `pi-dev` families and their `-pi-inference` gateway variants. A session lands on one of three compute kinds: `ec2`, `registered-host` or `k8s`. The dispatch path is identical for all three, and the launcher's last line is always `exec ark run-cursor`. ## How work flows

- **Jira ticket:** Work is created and tracked where the team already works.
- **Ark reads the ticket:** Ark pulls ticket context and linked docs, holds the credentials, and a planner agent drafts a plan.

# Onboarding 
Foundry runs coding agents on your team's repositories. You describe a piece of work, Foundry runs it through a defined process on a machine your team owns, and you get a pull request back. Many of those runs happen at once, on real hardware, rather than one at a time on your laptop.

It takes about an hour of your own time. The one thing you cannot do yourself is compute, which your DevOps sets up once for the whole team, so start that conversation early.

## Keeping a session affordable 
Token spend is dominated by **cache reads** , not by the visible input and output of a single turn, so a run can cost far more than its transcript suggests. A stage that carries a large context and then iterates re-reads that context every time.
Two things drive nearly every runaway run:
  - **Uncapped back-edges.** A reviewer that routes work back to an earlier stage will do it as many times as the flow allows. Set `max_iterations` on any stage with an `on_red` edge pointing back at it.
  - **An oversized context in the implementing stage.** Large files or accumulated artifacts pulled into a stage are re-read on every iteration of that stage.

Because the rate limit belongs to the credential rather than to one session, a single expensive run will stall every other agent resolving the same token. Stagger heavy runs, or giv

## What you get 
  - Parallel task execution: each session runs in a fresh, isolated environment (its own database, services, and Docker).
  - No local-machine bottleneck of one environment and one task at a time.
  - Feedback loops: reject at any stage and the agent reworks and retries (the retry cap is configurable, e.g. up to 8 before auto-reject).
  - **Artifacts** : inspect a flow's output at any stage while the session is still running.
  - **Manual gates** : approve or reject before a PR is raised, straight from Slack.
  - **Actions** : deterministic per-repo scripts (lint, test, build) so agents get consistent, typed results.
  - **Workspace hooks** : post-provision, post-clone, and post-services steps.

## How scope resolution works 
Secrets resolve **narrowest first** : user, then team, then tenant, and the first hit for each name wins. A team that sets nothing inherits the tenant default.
Two consequences worth knowing before you debug a missing secret:
  - Setting a value at **user** scope overrides team and tenant for your sessions only. That makes it the fastest way to unblock yourself while a shared value is being sorted out.
  - A team-scoped secret is matched by the team's canonical `tm-` id. A value stored against the team's name or slug will be visible in the UI and still not resolve at dispatch.

## Roles, and how a team comes online 
Onboarding a team comes down to one person. The platform team creates the accounts and gives one person a tenant-admin grant. From there that admin unlocks the rest for the team: they onboard everyone else, register the team's compute, and set the team's secrets, without the platform team in the loop for each step.
Ark has four roles:

Your role does not decide whether you can register a machine. It decides which rung the machine lands on, and the control plane reads that from the credential you enrol with:

## Registering on someone else's behalf 
`ark host enroll` calls the enrolment RPC every time it runs, and it enrols onto the caller's OWN rung. So handing someone the enroll command does not put the box where you meant it to go, and for a shared box it puts it somewhere they cannot reach.
The path that does work splits the credential from the command. An admin, team or tenant, mints the token, then the machine's owner starts the daemon with it. The owner needs no admin credential, because `ark host start` never calls the gated endpoint.
The admin mints it, either through the `compute` MCP tool with `op='register_host'`, or by running `ark host enroll <name>` and reading the token out of the host file. Send the token over a private channel, never a shared one. It is the enrollment secret and it grants fleet membership.

## Roles, and how a team comes online 
Onboarding a team comes down to one person. The platform team creates the accounts and gives one person a tenant-admin grant. ## Team-scoped secrets 
Teams can override identity secrets (Bitbucket bot user, own `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, JFrog account) for all their members at once - web UI → Secrets → Add secret → scope **team**.
Resolution is **user → team → tenant** , first hit per key wins; a team that sets nothing simply inherits tenant defaults. Team writes require a team-admin grant for that team (or tenant-admin).
WARNING
Never override infra values (`JIRA_BASE_URL`, JFrog URL, etc.) at team scope - it becomes invisible per-team configuration drift that looks like "Ark is broken only for our team."

## How scope resolution works 
Secrets resolve **narrowest first** : user, then team, then tenant, and the first hit for each name wins. A team that sets nothing inherits the tenant default.
Two consequences worth knowing before you debug a missing secret:
  - Setting a value at **user** scope overrides team and tenant for your sessions only. That makes it the fastest way to unblock yourself while a shared value is being sorted out.
  - A team-scoped secret is matched by the team's canonical `tm-` id. A value stored against the team's name or slug will be visible in the UI and still not resolve at dispatch.

## What your agents and workflows map to 
Three primitives make up a run, and your pre-made pieces map onto them:
  - **Agents** are agent definitions -- one worker with a model, a tool allow-list, a system prompt, and optional in-session subagents. Your "agents" become Ark agent definitions.
  - **Workflows** are flows -- a DAG of stages, where each stage is either an `agent` (a worker) or an `action` (a named workspace command). Stages hand typed artifacts to each other with `consumes:` / `produces:`, and `on_red:` back-edges route work backward for rework. Your "workflow" becomes an Ark flow.
  - **Workspaces** are repos plus tools, secrets, and named actions, materialised per session. A flow runs against a workspace on a compute, so the workspace is where your repo and your test/build/lint actions live.

**how long does it take to get set up and running my first session**

It takes about an hour of your own time total: 15 minutes to get access and connect, 20 minutes to set your personal credentials, 20 minutes to run your first session, and 5 minutes to link the Slack bot. [see: getting-started]

## What you get 
  - Parallel task execution: each session runs in a fresh, isolated environment (its own database, services, and Docker).

## How scope resolution works 
Secrets resolve **narrowest first** : user, then team, then tenant, and the first hit for each name wins. A team that sets nothing inherits the tenant default.
Two consequences worth knowing before you debug a missing secret:
  - Setting a value at **user** scope overrides team and tenant for your sessions only. That makes it the fastest way to unblock yourself while a shared value is being sorted out.
  - A team-scoped secret is matched by the team's canonical `tm-` id. A value stored against the team's name or slug will be visible in the UI and still not resolve at dispatch.

Account creation (Cognito login + tenant membership) is done by the platform team - send the email and team name (or a .csv for a whole team) to a tenant admin, listed on the **Settings** page under **Your admins**. Once the user exists, you control _what they can do_ with grants:

Onboarding a team comes down to one person. The platform team creates the accounts and gives one person a tenant-admin grant. ## Registering on someone else's behalf 
`ark host enroll` calls the enrolment RPC every time it runs, and it enrols onto the caller's OWN rung. So handing someone the enroll command does not put the box where you meant it to go, and for a shared box it puts it somewhere they cannot reach.
The path that does work splits the credential from the command. An admin, team or tenant, mints the token, then the machine's owner starts the daemon with it. The owner needs no admin credential, because `ark host start` never calls the gated endpoint.
The admin mints it, either through the `compute` MCP tool with `op='register_host'`, or by running `ark host enroll <name>` and reading the token out of the host file. Send the token over a private channel, never a shared one. It is the enrollment secret and it grants fleet membership.

### 0. Make Ark Reliable

**Goal:** Stop the outages before we add anything new.

- Stop 503s: credential-refresh grant for the weekly DB password rotation, plus event-consumer backpressure.
- Redis recovery, and managed EC2 or EKS instead of laptops.
- Team-scoped compute and credentials, with pre-flight prerequisite checks.
- Prevent an arkd disconnect from stranding a run; detect machine loss and recover.
- Do not kill a healthy long build, and surface no silent hangs.
- Pause and resume on a rate limit, and preserve work on every kill.
- Reduce UI polling, keep auth stable under load, and deliver Slack alarms.

**Done when:** No unannounced outage over 5 minutes, failures are fast and clear, arkd holds at normal load, healthy builds keep running, no silent hangs, the UI stays fast, no repeated logouts, no lost work, and alerts fire before users report.

## Decisions (these are decided, not open)

- **Compute:** Managed only. Laptops removed.
- **Local execution:** Revisit later through secure local-to-cloud portability.
- **Harness:** Standardise on Claude Agent. Cursor is secondary, run with the engineer's key.
- **Secrets and access:** Scope everything tightly: AWS secrets, session-scoped SSH, team and session scope, no cross-team access.
- **Infrastructure exposure:** Internal-only until every critical and high security finding closes.
- **Product sequencing:** Reliability before breadth.
- **Measurement:** Measure successful outcomes. Fix attribution first.
- **Roadmap and intake:** Publish the roadmap and run one shared tracker: problem, owner, priority, status, dependency, target and metric.
- **Communication:** Release notes in foundry-users, re-shared in all-engineer, with a weekly sum

### 3. Session Dispatch and Lifecycle

**Goal:** Every accepted dispatch runs or fails fast, with a clear reason.

- Fail-fast pre-flight that refuses in seconds when a prerequisite is missing.
- A subprocess-aware watchdog that does not kill a 30 to 40 minute Android build.
- Park and auto-resume on a rate limit, with the reset time shown.
- Clear state, reason, timeout, cancel and retry on every session.
- Detect and clean stranded sessions, and preserve work on every kill.
- Alert within minutes on a park, a stuck run, a disconnect or a dispatch failure.

**Done when:** Every accepted dispatch runs or fails in seconds with a clear reason, healthy builds survive, rate-limited runs resume, stranded sessions are cleaned, and no work is lost.

# Creating Kubernetes compute 
A `k8s` compute is not a machine. It is a pool row holding the cluster, the namespace, the pod image and the pod's resource limits, and every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. The pod runs `arkd` as its main container and dials out to the control plane, so nothing reaches into your cluster: no inbound route, no `kubectl port-forward`, no kubeconfig read at dispatch time. When the session ends the pod is deleted.
Because the pod is created per dispatch, a k8s pool is always cold. Setting a warm floor is rejected outright with `cannot be warm (min must be 0)`. There is nothing to keep warm.

You’re seeing two separate issues that often happen together.

1. **CLI and MCP report different tenants** – The CLI reads the active context from `~/.ark/config.yaml`, while the MCP uses the token that was minted when you registered the editor. If those tokens were created under different tenants, `ark auth whoami` and the MCP’s `auth/whoami` will each correctly show a different tenant.
   - Run `ark auth whoami` in a terminal.
   - In Claude Code (or Cursor) ask the MCP to run `auth/whoami` (e.g. type `/mcp` then `auth/whoami`).
   - Compare the tenant IDs.
   - If the MCP tenant isn’t listed in any of your local token files (`~/.claude.json`, `~/.claude/settings.json`, `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, `.cursor/mcp.json`), you’re dealing with a **stale connection** – simply restart your editor to clear the old registration.
   - If the tenant **is** listed, you have a **separate‑credential case** – the MCP is using a key that belongs to a different tenant. Mint a new user API key in the tenant you want (see step 2) and update the MCP registration, then restart the editor.

2. **API key is rejected** – This usually means the key you gave the MCP is either:
   - Not a **user API key** (e.g. a worker token minted by an enroll card), or
   - Minted under the wrong tenant, or
   - Corrupted/expired.
   
   Fix:
   - Open Ark’s web UI, go to **Settings → API Keys → Create key**, name it `mcp‑<yourname>` and copy the displayed `ark_t‑…_<hex>` value.
   - Verify the key works before touching the MCP config:
     ```bash
     curl -s https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/api/rpc \
          -X POST \
          -H "Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>" \
          -H 'content-type: application/json' \
          -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"auth/whoami","params":{}}'
     ```
   - The response should show your email and a role of `member`/`admin`. If you get `Unauthorized` or a role of `worker`, you used the wrong kind of token.
   - Update the MCP configuration with the new key:
     *In Claude Code*: run `/mcp`, choose **Add MCP**, paste the key, and confirm the connection.
     *In Cursor*: edit `.cursor/mcp.json` (or `~/.cursor/mcp.json`) to include:
     ```json
     {
       "mcpServers": {
         "ark": {
           "type": "http",
           "url": "https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/mcp",
           "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <YOUR_KEY>" }
         }
       }
     }
     ```
   - Restart the editor (or run `claude mcp remove ark && claude mcp add ...` if you have duplicate registrations) and run `auth/whoami` again to confirm the tenant matches the CLI.

After these steps, both the CLI and the MCP should report the same tenant, and the API key will be accepted.

Check the secret’s scope and definition. A *secret‑will‑not‑resolve* error means the workspace declared a secret that didn’t resolve at dispatch. Secrets are looked up in the narrowest scope first – user, then team, then tenant – and the first match wins. 

1. Open the Ark Secrets view and verify that the secret you need is set for **your user** (not at the team level) – a user‑scoped secret overrides team/tenant values and is the quickest way to unblock yourself. 
2. If you set the secret at team scope, make sure it was stored against the team’s canonical `tm‑` id, not its name or slug. 
3. Confirm the secret value isn’t expired (e.g., OAuth tokens like `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` rotate and will appear missing when stale). 
4. Remember there’s a ~10‑minute cache on secret changes; after adding or updating a secret, wait a few minutes and retry the session. 
5. Since you enrolled a MacBook, ensure the compute is healthy and scoped to your own user rung (personal laptops should be scoped to the user, not the team). Verify the box is online (`ark host status <name>` or `ark compute list`) and has capacity set.

By looking at the secret’s scope in the UI, confirming it matches the session’s team/user, and waiting for the cache to refresh, you can resolve the “secret will not resolve” error.

You can run Ark on a laptop, but the docs advise using managed EC2/EKS for reliable sessions. Laptops are supported only for personal use and often fail because they sleep, run out of disk, or drift. For a production‑grade setup you should provision an EC2 compute.

**Laptop enrollment**
1. The box must be Linux or macOS and be able to reach the Ark control‑plane on port 443.
2. Install the enrollment script and run it (you need a user API key from Settings):
   ```
   API_KEY=your‑user‑api‑key MACHINE_NAME=my‑laptop ./ark-enroll-host.sh
   ```
   The script installs the `ark` CLI, the session runtime (`bun` and Claude Code) if missing, logs you in, starts `arkd` on port 19300, registers the host as a systemd/LaunchAgent service, and sets its capacity (cores / 2 unless you override with `MAX_SESSIONS`, `RAM`, or `CPU`).
3. Capacity detection assumes about 100 GB of free disk; the docs note a 100 GB minimum for compute.
4. Scope the laptop to your own user‑rung so no other team member’s session lands on it.

**Provisioning an EC2 compute**
1. Your DevOps must set up two AWS pieces for the team:
   * VPC peering with the Ark account.
   * A cross‑account IAM role generated from the Ark **Connect** page (pick *provision* mode) that includes the required EC2, SSM, and `iam:PassRole` permissions.
2. Choose a shape – a dedicated box (single named instance) or a pool (template that launches a fresh instance per session). A solid default EC2 size is `m6i.2xlarge` (8 vCPU / 32 GB RAM).
3. Create the compute row, for example:
   ```
   ark compute create risk‑devbox \
     --kind ec2 \
     --instance-id i-0123456789abcdef0   # for adopt mode, omit for provision mode
   ```
   In provision mode you also supply `--role-arn` and `--external-id` from the generated role.
4. After the row exists, run `ark compute provision risk‑devbox` to launch the instance. The CLI will call `RunInstances`, wait for the SSM agent, install `arkd`, and set the row status to `running`.
5. The instance must have an outbound route to the Ark VPC (`10.72.216.0/23`) on port 443; no inbound ports are needed.
6. Capacity is roughly `cores ÷ 2`; an 8‑core box can host about four concurrent sessions.

**Bottom line**: Use a managed EC2/EKS compute for stable, team‑scoped sessions. Enrolling a laptop is possible for personal experimentation, but you need the enrollment script, a user API key, and a reliable network/disk environment.

You missed re‑initialising the MCP registration after the CLI upgrade. After updating, Claude Code still sees the old registration and the tools can’t be fetched. Fix it by cleaning up the duplicate MCP entry and restarting Claude Code:

1. List the current registrations:

3. Make sure the remaining entry points to the correct URL (ends with `/mcp`) and includes the proper header:
   ```bash
   claude mcp add --transport http ark \
     https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/mcp \
     --header "Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>"
   ```
4. Restart Claude Code (or quit and reopen it). The restart forces the MCP client to pick up the corrected registration.

   /mcp               # should report “connected” without tool fetch errors
   ```

   ```bash
   ark install-claude-code
   ```

# Creating EC2 compute 
An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. The same kind can also adopt a box you already run, in which case Foundry installs `arkd` and nothing else, as below. That is the difference from [registering a machine you already own](/onboarding/registering-compute), where the box dials in and Foundry never touches its lifecycle.
You create it in one of two shapes. A **dedicated box** is a single named instance your team's sessions land on, which is what most teams start with. A **pool** is a blueprint that cuts a fresh instance per session up to a ceiling you set, which is what you want once several people dispatch at once. Both are covered below; the sizing, capacity, and trou

## Capacity and admission 
Admission control decides how much work a box will accept before it queues the rest, and it is on by default. When a compute declares no `capacity`, Foundry derives a conservative one from the instance size at 85% headroom, reserving the rest for the OS, `arkd`, and the agent runtime. An `m` box (8 vCPU, 32 GB) therefore admits against roughly 27Gi and 680% CPU.
An adopted box carries no size, because Foundry did not choose its instance type and will not invent one, so declaring capacity is not optional there: until you do, a workspace that declares a `resource_budget` is refused on it with a message naming exactly this. A workspace declaring no budget is not gated at all, so an uncapped adopted box will accept work regardless.

You need to complete these prerequisites before you can run any session:
1. **Get access and connect** – have an Ark account, the `ark` MCP connected in your editor/CLI, and confirm it works with `ark auth whoami`.
2. **Set your personal credentials** – configure the SSH key you’ll use for source control (e.g. `ssh -i ~/.ssh/ark_bitbucket -T git@bitbucket.org`).
3. **Enroll a compute** – register a machine (EC2, registered‑host, or k8s pool), make sure it’s healthy, online, and has capacity set (`ark compute list/show`).
4. **Have a workspace** – a workspace definition that lists the repos to clone, tools to install, services to run, and any secrets the session needs (`ark workspace list` or `ark workspace show <name>`). You can test it with `ark workspace test` before dispatch.
5. **Choose a flow** – use a built‑in flow (e.g. `ark-feature`) or a flow you’ve registered. The flow, together with the workspace and compute, are required when you start a session.
Once those items are in place you can start your first session with a command such as:
```bash
ark session start [TICKET] \
  --flow <flow-name> \
  --workspace <workspace-name> \
  --compute <compute-name> \
  --summary "<short description>"
```
The command will print a session ID, indicating the session has been dispatched.

Yes. After you enroll a machine you control as a registered‑host, you can dispatch any flow you have registered to run on that compute.

1. **Enroll the machine** – on the box run a host‑enrollment command, for example:
   ```bash
   ark host enroll my‑box --isolation direct --detach
   ```
   (or have an admin mint a token with `ark host enroll` and give it to the box owner, who places it under `~/.ark/host/registered-host/...` and runs `ark host start`). The daemon `arkd` will start and dial out to the control plane.
2. **Scope the machine** – the credential you use decides the rung the box lands on (tenant‑admin → tenant rung, team‑admin → team rung, member → your own user rung). A member‑enrolled laptop is scoped to your user rung so only your sessions use it.
3. **Register the agents your flow needs** (once):
   ```bash
   ark agent create myteam-reviewer --from myteam-reviewer.yaml --global
   ```
4. **Apply a workspace** that contains your repo and tools:
   ```bash
   ark workspace apply myteam-workspace.yaml
   ```
5. **Validate and create the flow**:
   ```bash
   ark flow validate ./myteam-review.yaml --repo .
   ark flow create myteam-review --from ./myteam-review.yaml
   ```
6. **Start a session on the enrolled compute** – either via MCP (natural language) or the CLI:
   ```bash
   session_lifecycle(op='start', summary='review the auth refactor',
     flow='myteam-review', workspace='myteam-workspace', compute='my‑box')
   ```
   or
   ```bash
   ark session start --flow myteam-review --workspace myteam-workspace \
     --compute my‑box --summary "review the auth refactor"
   ```
The session will resolve the flow, materialise the workspace on your enrolled machine, and run the agents there. So your own registered flow can indeed run on a machine you enrolled yourself.

# Onboarding 
Foundry runs coding agents on your team's repositories. You describe a piece of work, Foundry runs it through a defined process on a machine your team owns, and you get a pull request back. Many of those runs happen at once, on real hardware, rather than one at a time on your laptop.

Your role does not decide whether you can register a machine. It decides which rung the machine lands on, and the control plane reads that from the credential you enrol with:
Your credential| Where the box lands| Who can use it  
---|---|---  
tenant-admin| the tenant rung| everyone in the tenant  
team-admin| your team's rung| your team's subtree  
member| your own user rung| you, plus your admins

An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. You can link your Slack identity to your Ark identity in two ways:

**Web UI (quickest)**
1. Open the **Onboarding** tab in the Ark web UI.
2. Click **Generate** on the **Connect Slack** card. This mints a one‑use Slack link token (no CLI or admin rights needed).
3. Open a direct message to the Ark bot in Slack and paste the token.
4. The bot will confirm that your accounts are linked and you can start using `/ark` commands.

**CLI (terminal‑only)**
1. Make sure you have a personal, identity‑bound user API key (mint one from Settings → API Keys if you don’t have it).
2. Run:
   ```
   ark slack link \
     --server https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com \
     --token <YOUR_ARK_API_KEY>
   ```
   This prints a 32‑character link token that expires in 15 minutes.
3. Immediately DM the Ark bot in Slack and send the token (or run `ark link <token>` inside the DM).
4. The bot will confirm the link and you can use `/ark` in any channel where the bot is invited.

**If linking is refused**
- **Permission denied (tenant.admin)** – This happens when you run `ark slack link --force`. The `--force` flag is a tenant‑admin action and will fail for a normal user. Run the plain `ark slack link` command (no `--force`) or use the web UI card.
- **Token expired or DM didn’t reach the bot** – The token is single‑use and only valid for 15 minutes. If you see “Your Slack account is not linked”, redo steps 2–3 to mint a fresh token and DM it again.
- **API key isn’t identity‑bound** – A shared or non‑user key causes the permission error. Mint a fresh user API key from Settings → API Keys and use that for the CLI command.
- **Cannot DM the bot** – Send your Slack member ID to a tenant admin so they can link the accounts for you.

Following these steps will connect the Ark Slack bot, and the troubleshooting items above cover the common refusal scenarios.

When a clone fails inside a session the most common reason is the SSH key, not the workspace definition itself. Ark checks the `repo cloned` step before any other workspace actions, and a failure there is reported as a credentials problem. You should:
1. Verify the key works from your own machine: `ssh -i ~/.ssh/ark_bitbucket -T git@bitbucket.org`. It must print “authenticated via ssh key”.
2. Store the **private** key (pass‑phrase‑free) in an Ark secret whose name matches the Bitbucket workspace of the repo, e.g. `BITBUCKET_SSH_KEY_PAYTMTEAM` for URLs like `bitbucket.org/paytmteam/...`. The suffix is required; using the wrong suffix produces `Permission denied (publickey)`.
3. Make sure the secret is scoped **user**, type **ssh‑private‑key**, and the username in the secret is `git`.
4. Confirm the repo is visible to that Bitbucket account (the key’s account must have access).
If those steps pass, the workspace YAML is likely fine; the clone error is coming from the SSH credential. (If you used the wrong secret name, that is a workspace‑level mistake that still shows up as an SSH failure.)

Planned: the platform is moving to fully managed, team‑scoped compute. Future releases will default to Managed EC2 or EKS instances, automatically provision VPC peering, enforce per‑session secret and file isolation, and remove the need for personal‑machine execution. The goal is that every session runs on approved, team‑scoped compute with credentials scoped to the right team.

Work‑around now: you can still run jobs by borrowing an existing shared compute (a running row or a pool) or by registering a server you control. List the available compute with `ark compute list`, pick a row whose STATUS is `running`, and dispatch your flow to it (you can also create a dedicated EC2 compute or adopt an existing instance if needed). This lets you run without waiting for the full managed compute rollout.

To fix this:
1. Verify your flow’s YAML uses `gate: manual` on the stage where you expect interaction. If it’s set to `gate: auto`, the run will proceed without prompting.
2. Make sure your Slack identity is linked to your Ark account – the last onboarding step. Open the **Onboarding** tab in the web UI, click **Generate** on the **Connect Slack** card, copy the link token, and DM it to the Slack bot (or follow the “Generate” flow in the UI). After linking, the bot will confirm the accounts are linked.

4. Once the bot is linked and a manual gate is defined, a run will pause at that gate, you’ll get a Slack DM, and you can approve/reject the session.

If you’ve already linked Slack (step 4 in the onboarding checklist) and the gate is manual but you still get no DM, double‑check that the Slack bot is installed in the workspace and that your Slack account can receive DMs from it. If everything looks correct, the run is behaving as designed (auto gate), so add a manual gate where you need a prompt.

Create an agent YAML that includes a `runtime: cursor` field. For example:
```yaml
name: my‑cursor‑worker   # kebab‑case name for the agent
runtime: cursor          # forces this worker to always run on the Cursor harness
# optional: model, system_prompt, tools, etc.
```
Save the file (e.g., `my‑cursor‑worker.yaml`) and register it with the CLI:
```bash
ark agent create my‑cursor‑worker --from my‑cursor‑worker.yaml --no-editor [--global]
ark agent list   # verify the agent appears
```
The `runtime` entry in the YAML makes the worker permanently bound to the Cursor harness, so every dispatch of this agent will run on Cursor without needing a per‑session override.

A `k8s` compute is not a machine. It is a pool row holding the cluster, the namespace, the pod image and the pod's resource limits, and every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. You need a few things on the Mac before any Cursor stage can run:

1. The Mac must already be enrolled as a *registered host* so that the Ark CLI is installed at `~/.ark/bin/ark` (the one‑click bridge assumes this). 
2. A working Node runtime and `npm` must be on the machine’s `PATH` – the Cursor SDK uses them to launch the stage.
3. The host needs internet egress to `nodejs.org` and the npm registry and a writable `$HOME` directory because Ark will provision a pinned Node in `~/.ark/runtime` and the Cursor SDK in `~/.ark/cursor-sdk` the first time a Cursor session runs.
4. Use a **user** token, not a machine token (the `whoami` role should be something like `user` rather than `worker`). If you see `"role":"worker"` you need to mint a fresh user key.
5. Ensure the repository you dispatch does **not** contain a `.cursor/mcp.json` or `.cursor/hooks.json` file – the Cursor runtime will refuse to start if those project‑level config files are present.
6. (Optional but helpful) Run `ark host doctor` to confirm the host can resolve the Cursor launcher and that all prerequisites are satisfied.

When those items are in place, Ark will automatically provision the runtime the first time you dispatch a Cursor‑pinned flow (e.g. `ark session start --flow cursor-smoke`).

Run `ark flow show <flow-name>` (or `ark flow list` then `ark flow show`) to view the wiring of each stage. In the output you’ll see lines such as `on_red -> <stage>` – those are back‑edges that let a stage send work backward to an earlier step. Any stage that has an `on_red:` edge is capable of routing work back.

To stop the run from looping forever, set a `max_iterations` value on the stage (or on the flow) that caps how many times that back‑edge may fire. When the limit is reached the run escalates instead of looping indefinitely. Adding `max_iterations` on every stage with an `on_red:` edge prevents unlimited re‑work loops.

So, check the flow definition for `on_red:` edges to know if a process can send work back, and use `max_iterations` to bound the number of times it can do so.

## Keeping a session affordable 
Token spend is dominated by **cache reads** , not by the visible input and output of a single turn, so a run can cost far more than its transcript suggests. A stage that carries a large context and then iterates re-reads that context every time.
Two things drive nearly every runaway run:
  - **Uncapped back-edges.** A reviewer that routes work back to an earlier stage will do it as many times as the flow allows. Set `max_iterations` on any stage with an `on_red` edge pointing back at it.
  - **An oversized context in the implementing stage.** Large files or accumulated artifacts pulled into a stage are re-read on every iteration of that stage.

## What you get 
  - Parallel task execution: each session runs in a fresh, isolated environment (its own database, services, and Docker).
  - No local-machine bottleneck of one environment and one task at a time.
  - Feedback loops: reject at any stage and the agent reworks and retries (the retry cap is configurable, e.g. up to 8 before auto-reject).

Secrets resolve **narrowest first** : user, then team, then tenant, and the first hit for each name wins. A team that sets nothing inherits the tenant default.

First check the health of the daemon on the box:
```
ark host doctor
```
If the doctor reports the worker is not registered, restart the daemon (systemd on Linux, LaunchAgent on macOS):
```
systemctl restart arkd   # Linux
launchctl unload /Library/LaunchAgents/com.arkd.plist && launchctl load /Library/LaunchAgents/com.arkd.plist   # macOS
```
If restarting does not bring the worker back, re‑enroll the machine, which mints a fresh token and registers the worker again:
```
ark host enroll <name>
```
(Replace `<name>` with the compute name you use.) Note that re‑enrolling cuts off any sessions currently running on that box, so do it when you can afford a brief interruption.
For a long‑lived box, enroll with a persistent service instead of `--detach` so the daemon survives reboots:
```
ark host enroll <name> --isolation direct --systemd   # Linux
ark host enroll <name> --isolation direct --launchd   # macOS
```

The platform team is aware that runs are lost when `arkd` disconnects. They have identified this as a current gap (503s, Redis loss, arkd disconnects, machine‑loss strand runs) and are building improvements such as credential‑refresh grants, back‑pressure handling, Redis recovery, and disconnect/machine‑loss recovery. The goal is to eliminate unannounced outages longer than five minutes and ensure no runs are lost due to a daemon drop‑off.

  - An Ark account. If you do not have one yet, follow [Getting Access](/onboarding/getting-access) first.

## Registering on someone else's behalf 
`ark host enroll` calls the enrolment RPC every time it runs, and it enrols onto the caller's OWN rung. So handing someone the enroll command does not put the box where you meant it to go, and for a shared box it puts it somewhere they cannot reach.
The path that does work splits the credential from the command. An admin, team or tenant, mints the token, then the machine's owner starts the daemon with it. The owner needs no admin credential, because `ark host start` never calls the gated endpoint.
The admin mints it, either through the `compute` MCP tool with `op='register_host'`, or by running `ark host enroll <name>` and reading the token out of the host file. Send the token over a private channel, never a shared one. It is the enrollment secret and it grants fleet membership.

At the moment Ark does not automatically import the agents and skills that are already in your repo. The existing AGENTS.md, agent definitions, and skills have to be registered manually. Create each agent with the CLI, for example:

Your agent YAML should include at least `name` and `runtime`, and typically also `model`, `system_prompt`, and `tools` (your skills). A minimal example:

name: myteam-reviewer
runtime: claude-agent
model: sonnet
system_prompt: |

tools:
  - Read
  - Grep
  - Bash
```

Future self‑serve onboarding (see the Aug 31 2026 roadmap) will detect and import these assets automatically, but until that feature ships you need to register each one by hand.

If Claude returns nothing it usually means the OAuth token it needs isn’t available. `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` is required for any workspace that uses Claude, and a missing or expired token is treated as “missing” – the agent will start but immediately have no model to call, so you see no output.

Fix it by minting a fresh token and adding it as a **user‑scoped** secret:

1. Run `claude setup-token` to create a new token.
2. In Ark, add the secret named `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` with the token value (user scope, not team scope).
3. Wait ~10 minutes for the secret cache to refresh, then dispatch your session again.

If you don’t have Claude access, you can instead run the flow on the Cursor runtime by setting `CURSOR_API_KEY` and using a workspace that does **not** declare `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`.

Token spend is dominated by **cache reads** , not by the visible input and output of a single turn, so a run can cost far more than its transcript suggests. A stage that carries a large context and then iterates re-reads that context every time.

To find out whether the failure comes from the compute box or from your workspace, follow these steps:

1. **Look at the session logs** – Open the session in the UI and view *Events → Output → Transcript* or check the CLI stdout transcript. Errors that mention missing secrets, a bad workspace, or a failed action point to a project‑setup issue. (Chunk 4)

2. **Check the health of the machine** – On the box run the health check:
   ```
   host doctor
   ```
   It will report if the health probe failed (missing tool, full disk, or arkd down). (Chunk 1, Chunk 3)

3. **Verify the compute registration** from any machine with your credentials:
   ```
   ark compute list
   ark compute show <machine-name>
   ```
   The listing shows whether the box is enrolled, its architecture, and its status. If it shows `Enrolled: yes` on the host but the control‑plane list does not reflect it, the machine is not reachable. (Chunk 19)

4. **Confirm capacity and resources** – The machine must have at least 100 GB free disk and 16 GB RAM (32 GB for large monorepos). If capacity isn’t set, the session will stay stuck. (Chunk 3)

5. **Inspect workspace definition** – A workspace defines actions, repos, tools, and secrets. Errors like `workspace_undoctored` or a missing secret indicate the workspace configuration is the problem, not the compute. (Chunk 10, Chunk 24)

6. **Isolate the cause** – If the logs show only health‑probe or tool‑missing messages and the host doctor reports problems, the machine is bad. If the logs complain about missing secrets, undefined actions, or workspace validation failures, the issue is in your project setup. You can also retry the same flow on a known‑good pool machine (`ark compute pool list` → pick a member) to see if it succeeds; a successful run on another machine confirms the original box was at fault.

By separating the logs, health check, compute listing, and workspace validation you can tell whether the failure is due to the compute environment or your project configuration.

Secrets resolve **narrowest first** : user, then team, then tenant, and the first hit for each name wins. A team that sets nothing inherits the tenant default.

A run that costs a lot usually blows up because the flow loops without a limit or pulls in a huge context that gets re‑read on every iteration. The two common culprits are:
1. **Uncapped back‑edges** – a stage that has an `on_red:` edge can be sent back repeatedly. If you don’t bound it, the run can keep looping and burn tokens.
2. **Oversized context** – large files or many artifacts kept in the stage are re‑read each time, adding token spend.

**What to set:**
- Add a `max_iterations` value to any stage that has a back‑edge (`on_red:`) so the loop stops after a defined number of retries.
- Trim the context your stage consumes or limit the size of artifacts/files it loads, keeping only what’s needed for that stage.

These two steps will prevent runaway token usage and keep runs affordable.

## A pool instead of a box

alId=ark-cross-account-<slug>
Dispatch picks a member in a fixed order: the running member with the most free capacity (ties broken least-recently-used), else a stopped member which the dispatch path wakes, else a fresh member launched from the pool config, up to `--max`. At the ceiling with everything saturated, dispatch fails with `at max capacity`, so `--max` is a real cost limit and not a hint. One member hosts one session unless you raise `capacity.max_sessions` on the pool.

3. Register it with the CLI:
   ```
   ark flow create my‑flow --from ./my‑flow.yaml
   ```
4. (Optional) List your flows with `ark flow list` to confirm it appears.
You typically do this after you’ve run a built‑in flow once (so you have a session and the necessary credentials), then you can author and register your own custom flow for your team’s process.

# Creating EC2 compute 
An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. # Set up Cursor 
Cursor shows up in Foundry in two unrelated ways, and this page covers both.
The first is Cursor as your editor: it connects to the control plane's MCP server and gets the `ark` toolbox, so you can dispatch sessions, inspect flows and steer runs without leaving Cursor. The second is Cursor as a **runtime** , one of the harnesses Foundry dispatches agents onto, alongside the `claude-agent` and `pi-dev` families and their `-pi-inference` gateway variants. In that mode nobody is sitting in the editor at all: a stage runs on Cursor's agent SDK, on an EC2 box, a registered host or in a Kubernetes pod, and reports back like any other stage.

After a new release lands you should verify that you’re on the updated CLI and plugin, that your editor‑side connection is still alive, and that any tenant workspace you’ll use is applied with the correct namespace. Specifically:
1. Re‑pull the `ark` binary and the `ark‑superpowers` Claude Code plugin so you have the newest commands and agent view.
2. Restart Claude Code so the plugin reloads.
3. Run `/mcp` (or `ark whoami`) to confirm the CLI still reports a connected, healthy session.
4. If the marketplace re‑add fails because of authentication, mint a fresh API key and run `ark login` again, then repeat the `/mcp` check.
5. When applying a tenant workspace on the new release, include the `--namespace <token>` flag (or `--legacy` for pre‑namespace workspaces) so the name is correctly prefixed.
6. Finally, double‑check you have the latest Ark version before dispatching any session.
Doing these steps ensures the CLI, plugin, auth token, and workspace namespace are all aligned before you dispatch a new session.

# Updating the Ark CLI & plugin 
The `ark` binary and the `ark-superpowers` Claude Code plugin ship from the control plane, so they move forward as the platform does. When a release lands you re-pull both: the CLI to pick up new commands and fixes, the plugin so Claude Code sees the current agents, flows, and skills. This page is the update path once you already have an account and a working `ark login`. If you have not set either up yet, start at [Getting Access + MCP](/onboarding/getting-access).

### 0. Make Ark Reliable

**Goal:** Stop the outages before we add anything new.

- Stop 503s: credential-refresh grant for the weekly DB password rotation, plus event-consumer backpressure.
- Redis recovery, and managed EC2 or EKS instead of laptops.
- Team-scoped compute and credentials, with pre-flight prerequisite checks.
- Prevent an arkd disconnect from stranding a run; detect machine loss and recover.
- Do not kill a healthy long build, and surface no silent hangs.
- Pause and resume on a rate limit, and preserve work on every kill.
- Reduce UI polling, keep auth stable under load, and deliver Slack alarms.

**Done when:** No unannounced outage over 5 minutes, failures are fast and clear, arkd holds at normal load, healthy builds keep running, no silent hangs, the UI stays fast, no repeated logouts, no lost work, and alerts fire before users report.

## Decisions (these are decided, not open)

- **Compute:** Managed only. Laptops removed.
- **Local execution:** Revisit later through secure local-to-cloud portability.
- **Harness:** Standardise on Claude Agent. Cursor is secondary, run with the engineer's key.
- **Secrets and access:** Scope everything tightly: AWS secrets, session-scoped SSH, team and session scope, no cross-team access.
- **Infrastructure exposure:** Internal-only until every critical and high security finding closes.
- **Product sequencing:** Reliability before breadth.
- **Measurement:** Measure successful outcomes. Fix attribution first.
- **Roadmap and intake:** Publish the roadmap and run one shared tracker: problem, owner, priority, status, dependency, target and metric.
- **Communication:** Release notes in foundry-users, re-shared in all-engineer, with a weekly sum

### 3. Session Dispatch and Lifecycle

**Goal:** Every accepted dispatch runs or fails fast, with a clear reason.

- Fail-fast pre-flight that refuses in seconds when a prerequisite is missing.
- A subprocess-aware watchdog that does not kill a 30 to 40 minute Android build.
- Park and auto-resume on a rate limit, with the reset time shown.
- Clear state, reason, timeout, cancel and retry on every session.
- Detect and clean stranded sessions, and preserve work on every kill.
- Alert within minutes on a park, a stuck run, a disconnect or a dispatch failure.

**Done when:** Every accepted dispatch runs or fails in seconds with a clear reason, healthy builds survive, rate-limited runs resume, stranded sessions are cleaned, and no work is lost.

## Getting help 
When you report a problem, send the exact command and its exact output, plus the session id. A session id lets whoever picks it up read the event trail directly, and it saves a round trip that usually costs an hour.
Check whether the control plane itself is degraded before deep-diving your own setup. A broad outage produces 503s, socket errors, sessions stuck mid-stage and workers dropping offline all at once, and it is announced in the channel.

## After you update 
Restart Claude Code for the plugin update to take effect, then run `/mcp` to confirm `ark` still reports connected. If the marketplace re-add failed on authentication, your stored token is stale: remint a key and run `ark login` again, then re-run the update. The commands and identity check are the same ones covered under [Getting Access + MCP](/onboarding/getting-access).

### Step 4: network path from your pods back to the control plane 
Every session pod runs `arkd`, which dials `controlPlaneUrl` outward and registers. This direction is easy to overlook because nothing in steps 1 to 3 exercises it, and it fails late: the pool creates fine, pods start, and the session then waits for an agent that never attached.

      https://ark.internal.ap-so

# Creating Kubernetes compute 
A `k8s` compute is not a machine. It is a pool row holding the cluster, the namespace, the pod image and the pod's resource limits, and every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. The pod runs `arkd` as its main container and dials out to the control plane, so nothing reaches into your cluster: no inbound route, no `kubectl port-forward`, no kubeconfig read at dispatch time. When the session ends the pod is deleted.
Because the pod is created per dispatch, a k8s pool is always cold. Setting a warm floor is rejected outright with `cannot be warm (min must be 0)`. There is nothing to keep warm.

## Sizing

100`, so `1600` is sixteen cores. It is the one place that does not take Kubernetes units: a value like `28000m` does not parse and the CPU half of the ceiling is silently dropped, while `resources.cpu` on the same row is Kubernetes-style and does take `500m`.
Tool caching takes one decision. By default each workspace gets a ReadWriteOnce PVC that stays warm between sessions but pins concurrent sessions for that workspace to one node. Set `toolCacheMode` to `s3` for a fleet with S3 storage configured, which keeps the cache warm with no node affinity at all, or to `per-session` for a cold cache and unbounded concurrency.

# Onboarding 
Foundry runs coding agents on your team's repositories. You describe a piece of work, Foundry runs it through a defined process on a machine your team owns, and you get a pull request back. Many of those runs happen at once, on real hardware, rather than one at a time on your laptop.
This section gets you from nothing to your first run. You will need an account, your editor connected, and a few credentials so the work is done as you and not as a shared account.
It takes about an hour of your own time. The one thing you cannot do yourself is compute, which your DevOps sets up once for the whole team, so start that conversation early.

Secrets resolve **narrowest first** : user, then team, then tenant, and the first hit for each name wins. A team that sets nothing inherits the tenant default.

## Capacity and admission 
Admission control decides how much work a box will accept before it queues the rest, and it is on by default. When a compute declares no `capacity`, Foundry derives a conservative one from the instance size at 85% headroom, reserving the rest for the OS, `arkd`, and the agent runtime. An `m` box (8 vCPU, 32 GB) therefore admits against roughly 27Gi and 680% CPU.
An adopted box carries no size, because Foundry did not choose its instance type and will not invent one, so declaring capacity is not optional there: until you do, a workspace that declares a `resource_budget` is refused on it with a message naming exactly this. A workspace declaring no budget is not gated at all, so an uncapped adopted box will accept work regardless.

## Keeping a session affordable 
Token spend is dominated by **cache reads** , not by the visible input and output of a single turn, so a run can cost far more than its transcript suggests. A stage that carries a large context and then iterates re-reads that context every time.
Two things drive nearly every runaway run:

  - **An oversized context in the implementing stage.** Large files or accumulated artifacts pulled into a stage are re-read on every iteration of that stage.

Secrets resolve **narrowest first** : user, then team, then tenant, and the first hit for each name wins. A team that sets nothing inherits the tenant default.

## Registering on someone else's behalf 
`ark host enroll` calls the enrolment RPC every time it runs, and it enrols onto the caller's OWN rung. So handing someone the enroll command does not put the box where you meant it to go, and for a shared box it puts it somewhere they cannot reach.
The path that does work splits the credential from the command. An admin, team or tenant, mints the token, then the machine's owner starts the daemon with it. The owner needs no admin credential, because `ark host start` never calls the gated endpoint.

The first is Cursor as your editor: it connects to the control plane's MCP server and gets the `ark` toolbox, so you can dispatch sessions, inspect flows and steer runs without leaving Cursor. ## Keeping a session affordable 
Token spend is dominated by **cache reads** , not by the visible input and output of a single turn, so a run can cost far more than its transcript suggests. A stage that carries a large context and then iterates re-reads that context every time.

# Onboarding 
Foundry runs coding agents on your team's repositories. You describe a piece of work, Foundry runs it through a defined process on a machine your team owns, and you get a pull request back. Many of those runs happen at once, on real hardware, rather than one at a time on your laptop.
This section gets you from nothing to your first run. You will need an account, your editor connected, and a few credentials so the work is done as you and not as a shared account.
It takes about an hour of your own time. The one thing you cannot do yourself is compute, which your DevOps sets up once for the whole team, so start that conversation early.

- Managed EC2 and EKS supported, laptops removed, Claude Agent standard.
- Core Bitbucket and Jira connectivity, and AWS secrets.
- Pre-flight checks and full observability.
- Basic workspace setup, session recovery and rate-limit handling.
- Slack alert delivery and a cost-reporting foundation.

## How scope resolution works 
Secrets resolve **narrowest first** : user, then team, then tenant, and the first hit for each name wins. A team that sets nothing inherits the tenant default.
Two consequences worth knowing before you debug a missing secret:
  - Setting a value at **user** scope overrides team and tenant for your sessions only. That makes it the fastest way to unblock yourself while a shared value is being sorted out.
  - A team-scoped secret is matched by the team's canonical `tm-` id. A value stored against the team's name or slug will be visible in the UI and still not resolve at dispatch.

## 6\. Secrets 
**6.1 "How to add a secret?"** Ark UI → Secrets → User scope.
**6.2 "User scope vs Team scope -- which one?"** User = yours, and it overrides the shared default for your sessions (so PRs are authored as you). Team = shared default for the team. Personal creds always go at User scope -- putting them at Team scope overwrites your teammates.
**6.3 "How does Ark decide which secret to use?"** Narrowest wins: user → team → tenant. Secrets are injected per session, scoped to that session's environment, never global. So on a shared box, one person's session secrets don't leak into another's.
**6.4 "I added it but Ark is not able to find the secret."** There's a ~10-minute cache (temp fix for a propagation gap). Wait it out and retry before assuming it's broken.
**6.5 "Which secrets are mandatory?"** `JIRA_USER_EMAIL`, `JIRA_API_TOKEN`, `CONFLUENCE_API_TOKEN` \+ b

## Telling a cursor session apart 
The session detail page is the quickest answer. A cursor session carries a harness badge in the header and a `RUNTIME cursor` pair in the meta strip beneath it:
The sessions **list** is not a reliable surface for this. Its rows never carry the harness: the list labels a row from the agent name, and the web UI additionally asks for a trimmed projection that keeps only the keys a row renders. Open the session to be sure.

## Capacity and admission

ring no budget is not gated at all, so an uncapped adopted box will accept work regardless.
Declare it explicitly whenever you want a different ceiling, and always on an adopted box:
bash
    
    ark compute update risk-devbox \
      --set capacity.memory=24Gi \

The CLI and MCP are using different credentials, so the MCP is authenticating with a token that belongs to another tenant or is stale, and the key stored in the MCP is being rejected by the server.
Run `ark auth whoami` to see the CLI tenant.
In your editor, run `auth/whoami` on the MCP (e.g., `/mcp` then `auth/whoami`) to see the MCP tenant.
If the tenants differ because the MCP token is for the wrong tenant, mint a new user API key in the tenant you want (Settings → API Keys → Create key) and update the MCP registration with it.
If the tenants differ because the MCP is using a stale connection, fully restart your editor to clear the old registration.
Verify the new key works by calling the control plane:
`curl -s https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/api/rpc -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"auth/whoami","params":{}}'` and ensure the response shows your email and a member/admin role.
After updating the MCP config with the verified key, run `/mcp` (or the appropriate add command) and confirm it shows connected and the correct tenant.
If that does not work: make sure you are on the corporate network or VPN.

Your role does not decide whether you can register a machine. It decides which rung the machine lands on, and the control plane reads that from the credential you enrol with:

# Creating EC2 compute 
An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. The same kind can also adopt a box you already run, in which case Foundry installs `arkd` and nothing else, as below. That is the difference from [registering a machine you already own](/onboarding/registering-compute), where the box dials in and Foundry never touches its lifecycle.
You create it in one of two shapes. A **dedicated box** is a single named instance your team's sessions land on, which is what most teams start with. A **pool** is a blueprint that cuts a fresh instance per session up to a ceiling you set, which is what you want once several people dispatch at once. Both are covered below; the sizing, capacity, and trou

## Capacity and admission 
Admission control decides how much work a box will accept before it queues the rest, and it is on by default. When a compute declares no `capacity`, Foundry derives a conservative one from the instance size at 85% headroom, reserving the rest for the OS, `arkd`, and the agent runtime. An `m` box (8 vCPU, 32 GB) therefore admits against roughly 27Gi and 680% CPU.

A k8s compute is not a machine but a pool row holding the cluster, namespace, pod image and resource limits, where every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. [see: k8s-compute]

# Creating Kubernetes compute 
A `k8s` compute is not a machine. It is a pool row holding the cluster, the namespace, the pod image and the pod's resource limits, and every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. The pod runs `arkd` as its main container and dials out to the control plane, so nothing reaches into your cluster: no inbound route, no `kubectl port-forward`, no kubeconfig read at dispatch time. When the session ends the pod is deleted.
Because the pod is created per dispatch, a k8s pool is always cold. Setting a warm floor is rejected outright with `cannot be warm (min must be 0)`. There is nothing to keep warm.

The four nouns everything is built from are a **compute** (where a run happens), a **workspace** (your project made real: repos, tools, secrets, actions), a **flow** (the delivery process written down as stages), and a **session** (one run of a flow on a workspace on a compute). Steps 2 through 4 pick each of the first three; step 5 puts them together into a session.
Most people drive Ark from Claude Code in plain English, so each step below shows the natural-language MCP phrasing alongside the `ark` CL

When you report a problem, send the exact command and its exact output, plus the session id. A session id lets whoever picks it up read the event trail directly, and it saves a round trip that usually costs an hour.

# Onboarding 
Foundry runs coding agents on your team's repositories. You describe a piece of work, Foundry runs it through a defined process on a machine your team owns, and you get a pull request back. Many of those runs happen at once, on real hardware, rather than one at a time on your laptop.
This section gets you from nothing to your first run. You will need an account, your editor connected, and a few credentials so the work is done as you and not as a shared account.
It takes about an hour of your own time. The one thing you cannot do yourself is compute, which your DevOps sets up once for the whole team, so start that conversation early.

## Keeping a session affordable 
Token spend is dominated by **cache reads** , not by the visible input and output of a single turn, so a run can cost far more than its transcript suggests. A stage that carries a large context and then iterates re-reads that context every time.
Two things drive nearly every runaway run:
  - **Uncapped back-edges.** A reviewer that routes work back to an earlier stage will do it as many times as the flow allows. Set `max_iterations` on any stage with an `on_red` edge pointing back at it.
  - **An oversized context in the implementing stage.** Large files or accumulated artifacts pulled into a stage are re-read on every iteration of that stage.

Because the rate limit belongs to the credential rather than to one session, a single expensive run will stall every other agent resolving the same token. Stagger heavy runs, or giv

## What you get 
  - Parallel task execution: each session runs in a fresh, isolated environment (its own database, services, and Docker).
  - No local-machine bottleneck of one environment and one task at a time.
  - Feedback loops: reject at any stage and the agent reworks and retries (the retry cap is configurable, e.g. up to 8 before auto-reject).
  - **Artifacts** : inspect a flow's output at any stage while the session is still running.
  - **Manual gates** : approve or reject before a PR is raised, straight from Slack.
  - **Actions** : deterministic per-repo scripts (lint, test, build) so agents get consistent, typed results.
  - **Workspace hooks** : post-provision, post-clone, and post-services steps.

Ark does not replace Jira, Bitbucket, or a team's process; Jira stays where work is created and tracked, Bitbucket stays where code and review live, and Ark runs the agent workflow between them. [see: roadmap]

No; the decision is to remove laptops and use managed compute only, with managed EC2 or EKS as the default. [see: roadmap]

## Registering on someone else's behalf 
`ark host enroll` calls the enrolment RPC every time it runs, and it enrols onto the caller's OWN rung. So handing someone the enroll command does not put the box where you meant it to go, and for a shared box it puts it somewhere they cannot reach.
The path that does work splits the credential from the command. An admin, team or tenant, mints the token, then the machine's owner starts the daemon with it. The owner needs no admin credential, because `ark host start` never calls the gated endpoint.
The admin mints it, either through the `compute` MCP tool with `op='register_host'`, or by running `ark host enroll <name>` and reading the token out of the host file. Send the token over a private channel, never a shared one. It is the enrollment secret and it grants fleet membership.

A `k8s` compute is not a machine. It is a pool row holding the cluster, the namespace, the pod image and the pod's resource limits, and every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. ## Sizing 
Four numbers decide pod size and throughput, and none of them substitutes for another:
Field| What it sets  
---|---  
`config.resources`| The `arkd` container's request and limit, in Kubernetes units (`"2"` is two cores, `"500m"` half of one). Applies when the session declares no budget of its own  
workspace `resource_budget`| What actually sizes the pod on a real dispatch, so a workspace can outgrow the pool default  
`config.sidecarResources`| Charged once per declared service, plus one for DinD, in the same pod  
`config.capacity`| The admission ledger's ceiling for the whole pool row  
The pod total is `arkd` plus every sidecar, and that total has to fit on one node after daemonsets and kube-reserved take their share, which is meaningfully less than the instance spec suggests. A workspace that asks for slightly more than a node can give never schedules at all

### 0. Make Ark Reliable

**Goal:** Stop the outages before we add anything new.

- Stop 503s: credential-refresh grant for the weekly DB password rotation, plus event-consumer backpressure.
- Redis recovery, and managed EC2 or EKS instead of laptops.
- Team-scoped compute and credentials, with pre-flight prerequisite checks.
- Prevent an arkd disconnect from stranding a run; detect machine loss and recover.
- Do not kill a healthy long build, and surface no silent hangs.
- Pause and resume on a rate limit, and preserve work on every kill.
- Reduce UI polling, keep auth stable under load, and deliver Slack alarms.

**Done when:** No unannounced outage over 5 minutes, failures are fast and clear, arkd holds at normal load, healthy builds keep running, no silent hangs, the UI stays fast, no repeated logouts, no lost work, and alerts fire before users report.

## Decisions (these are decided, not open)

- **Compute:** Managed only. Laptops removed.
- **Local execution:** Revisit later through secure local-to-cloud portability.

- **Secrets and access:** Scope everything tightly: AWS secrets, session-scoped SSH, team and session scope, no cross-team access.
- **Infrastructure exposure:** Internal-only until every critical and high security finding closes.

**Goal:** Every accepted dispatch runs or fails fast, with a clear reason.

- Fail-fast pre-flight that refuses in seconds when a prerequisite is missing.
- A subprocess-aware watchdog that does not kill a 30 to 40 minute Android build.
- Park and auto-resume on a rate limit, with the reset time shown.
- Clear state, reason, timeout, cancel and retry on every session.
- Detect and clean stranded sessions, and preserve work on every kill.
- Alert within minutes on a park, a stuck run, a disconnect or a dispatch failure.

Personal laptops are being withdrawn

# Set up Cursor 
Cursor shows up in Foundry in two unrelated ways, and this page covers both.
The first is Cursor as your editor: it connects to the control plane's MCP server and gets the `ark` toolbox, so you can dispatch sessions, inspect flows and steer runs without leaving Cursor. The second is Cursor as a **runtime** , one of the harnesses Foundry dispatches agents onto, alongside the `claude-agent` and `pi-dev` families and their `-pi-inference` gateway variants. In that mode nobody is sitting in the editor at all: a stage runs on Cursor's agent SDK, on an EC2 box, a registered host or in a Kubernetes pod, and reports back like any other stage.
If you only want to drive Foundry from your editor, read to the end of Use it and then skip to Notes and gotchas. If you are running flows on the Cursor harness, the sections from Cursor as an agent harness onward are the ones you need.

No environment variable turns Cursor on, and looking for one is the most common wrong turn.
